summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. The annual dossiers of the national trans movement put numbers on that gap: CNN Brasil reported on 27 January 2025 that 122 trans and travesti people were killed in Brazil in 2024, a figure 16% below 2023, and SBT News reported on 26 January 2026 that ANTRA's 9th annual dossier counted 80 killings in 2025, a fall of roughly 34% year-on-year. Alagoas accounted for 6 of the 122 killings in 2024 and 2 of the 80 in 2025.

Brazil ranked first in the world for the killing of trans people for a 16th consecutive year in the 2024 dossier and remained at the top of world rankings in the 2025 count. The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence; in 2024 they were mostly young Black women, many from the Northeast, the region Alagoas belongs to.

Alagoas's own totals are small in absolute terms, so a few cases move the state's position sharply between consecutive annual counts, and the national totals themselves fell by about a third across the same two dossiers while Brazil kept the leading world ranking. For a visibly trans visitor, the hazard documented here is lethal violence directed at travestis and trans women, most of them young and Black, carried out with extreme force.
tangentialFactors:
ANTRA's dossier is the country's standing count of trans and travesti killings and has run for nine annual editions; the two most recent figures, 122 for 2024 and 80 for 2025, both represent year-on-year declines of 16% and roughly 34% respectively, yet Brazil held first place in world rankings in each.

Violence is not confined to homicide. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Courts have applied the hate-crime provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the nationwide rules on legal status: the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013, and the 2019 Supreme Court ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism for the purposes of constitutional and federal criminal provisions.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

Residents of Alagoas live under the same national violence record as the rest of the country: 6 trans and travesti people were killed in the state in 2024 and 2 in 2025, out of national totals of 122 and 80.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Alagoas-specific legal restriction, enforcement finding, hate-crime conviction count or police-practice record appears in the sources assembled here; the state-level material consists of the two ANTRA killing counts, 6 for 2024 and 2 for 2025.

Whether the fall from 122 killings nationally in 2024 to 80 in 2025 reflects reduced violence, changes in recording, or violence shifting into forms the dossier does not count is unresolved in these sources.

The prison census cited above covers eleven units in the Rio de Janeiro state system only, and its findings on housing in masculine-denominated units are not sourced for Alagoas prisons; how Resolution 348 and Resolution 366 are applied in Alagoas custody hearings is not documented here.

The nightclub entry refusal and the drink-spiking investigation both concern São Paulo, and no equivalent Alagoas case on commercial refusal of entry or nightlife targeting is available in this inventory. Entry, visa and document-screening practice specific to Alagoas airports or borders is not sourced; the nationwide equality of treatment at entry rests on the April 2026 expat legal guide rather than on Alagoas-level material.
